indicators.indicator_source_text: Create a shared vision and culture for using technology to learn and accelerate transformation through the coaching process.
met_criteria: Facilitates co-creation of a technology vision rather than presenting one
Builds a coaching culture where the vision is owned by educators, not prescribed
Uses the coaching process to align individual goals to the shared vision
Reviews and evolves the vision with stakeholders over time
not_yet_met_criteria: Communicates the institutional technology vision but does not facilitate shared ownership
Coaching is about compliance with adopted tools, not about building a learning culture
partial_indicators: Facilitates a vision workshop but does not maintain coaching practices that keep the vision alive in daily work
Builds individual buy-in from coached educators but does not connect this to a collective, sustained culture

indicators.indicator_source_text: Facilitate equitable use of digital learning tools and content that meet the needs of each learner.
met_criteria: Proactively identifies which students are not equitably served by current digital tool choices
Coaches educators to redesign for equity, not just access
Evaluates tools against equity criteria (accessibility, bias, language support)
Advocates for procurement and deployment decisions that serve all learners
not_yet_met_criteria: Works with the tools that are available without questioning their equity implications
Equity in tool use is seen as an IT or admin responsibility, not a coaching one
partial_indicators: Recommends accessible tools when a specific student need is flagged but does not proactively audit equity across the tool ecosystem
Ensures physical device access but does not examine whether tools serve diverse learner needs equitably

indicators.indicator_source_text: Cultivate a supportive coaching culture that encourages educators and leaders to achieve a shared vision and individual goals.
met_criteria: Creates psychological safety for educators to try, fail, and learn with technology
Celebrates growth, not just success
Connects individual coaching goals to the collective vision
Coaches leaders as well as classroom practitioners
not_yet_met_criteria: Coaching culture is evaluative rather than supportive
Educators feel monitored rather than supported
Individual coaching goals are disconnected from any shared direction
partial_indicators: Is personally supportive in one-to-one coaching conversations but has not built a culture of collective support and risk-taking across the institution
Connects individual goals to each other informally but does not facilitate a shared vision that educators own collectively

indicators.indicator_source_text: Recognize educators across the organization who use technology effectively to enable high-impact teaching and learning.
met_criteria: Establishes or contributes to formal mechanisms for recognising effective technology use
Recognition is tied to learning impact, not just tool adoption
Ensures recognition reaches beyond the self-selecting innovative educators to the broader staff
Uses recognition to model what high-impact technology use looks like
not_yet_met_criteria: Effective practice is not formally recognised — only failures or violations are highlighted
Recognition is informal and inconsistent
Does not use recognition as a professional learning or culture-building tool
partial_indicators: Verbally acknowledges good practice in coaching conversations but does not create visible, organisation-wide recognition
Highlights good practice in CPD sessions but this is not sustained or systematised

indicators.indicator_source_text: Connect leaders, educators, instructional support, technical support, domain experts and solution providers to maximize the potential of technology for learning.
met_criteria: Acts as a connector across the system — not just between educators
Brings technical and pedagogical stakeholders together around shared learning goals
Establishes or facilitates communities that include multiple stakeholder types
Uses their position to facilitate partnerships that individual educators could not access alone
not_yet_met_criteria: Coaching is entirely within the educator layer — does not engage technical, leadership, or external stakeholders
Does not use their role as a connector across the broader ecosystem
partial_indicators: Connects educators with each other through peer learning structures but does not bridge to technical support, leaders, or external solution providers
Attends cross-stakeholder meetings but does not facilitate connections that advance learning goals

indicators.indicator_source_text: Pursue professional learning that deepens expertise in the ISTE Standards in order to serve as a model for educators and leaders.
met_criteria: Has a clear and current understanding of all relevant ISTE Standards
Can articulate how the ISTE Standards connect to instructional practice
Pursues learning that deepens this expertise beyond surface familiarity
Models ISTE Standards-aligned practice in their own work
not_yet_met_criteria: Uses the ISTE Standards as a reference document but has not deepened expertise in applying them
Cannot serve as a model for others in ISTE Standards-aligned practice
partial_indicators: Is familiar with the ISTE Standards and references them in coaching but has not pursued deep expertise or used them systematically to frame their own practice as a model

indicators.indicator_source_text: Actively participate in professional learning networks to enhance coaching practice and keep current with emerging technology and innovations in pedagogy and the learning sciences.
met_criteria: Is an active (contributing) member of at least one professional learning network
Uses network participation to discover and evaluate emerging technologies
Connects network learning to changes in their coaching practice
Shares their own learning and practice with their network
not_yet_met_criteria: Professional learning is institution-based only
Does not participate in external networks or communities of practice
partial_indicators: Is a member of professional networks but primarily consumes rather than actively participates
Attends conferences but does not maintain ongoing network engagement between events

indicators.indicator_source_text: Establish shared goals with educators, reflect on successes and continually improve coaching and teaching practice.
met_criteria: Uses structured goal-setting with each educator at the start of a coaching cycle
Holds mid-cycle and end-of-cycle reflections with coached educators
Uses these reflections to adjust their own coaching practice — not just the teacher's
Documents what they are changing and why in their coaching approach
not_yet_met_criteria: Coaching is delivered without explicit shared goal-setting
Does not formally reflect on coaching outcomes or change practice based on them
partial_indicators: Sets goals with educators at the start of a coaching relationship but does not return to them systematically or use reflection to improve coaching practice itself

indicators.indicator_source_text: Establish trusting and respectful coaching relationships that encourage educators to explore new instructional strategies.
met_criteria: Invests explicit time in relationship-building before introducing coaching challenges
Creates conditions where educators feel safe to experiment and fail
Trust is evident in the educator's willingness to take instructional risks
Respects educator autonomy while maintaining coaching challenge and stretch
not_yet_met_criteria: Moves to instructional challenge without building relational trust
Educators in coaching relationships play it safe rather than experimenting
The coaching relationship is professional but not psychologically safe
partial_indicators: Is personally warm and respectful but has not created the depth of trust needed for educators to take genuine instructional risks with technology

indicators.indicator_source_text: Partner with educators to identify digital learning content that is culturally relevant, developmentally appropriate and considers student interests and aspirations.
met_criteria: Helps educators evaluate digital content against cultural relevance criteria for their specific students
Considers developmental appropriateness as a content selection criterion, not just curriculum alignment
Includes student interests and aspirations in the content selection conversation
Challenges choices of digital content that are culturally narrow or misaligned with student context
not_yet_met_criteria: Content recommendations are made without reference to the specific cultural, developmental, or aspirational context of the students
Defaults to popular or award-winning tools without contextualising for student population
partial_indicators: Recommends content that is developmentally appropriate and curriculum-aligned but does not specifically examine cultural relevance or connection to student interests and aspirations

indicators.indicator_source_text: Partner with educators to evaluate the efficacy of digital learning content and tools to inform procurement decisions and adoption.
met_criteria: Helps educators design and conduct evidence-based evaluations of tools in use
Contributes evaluation findings to procurement decision processes
Evaluation criteria include student learning impact, not just teacher satisfaction
Participates in procurement conversations with evidence-grounded recommendations
not_yet_met_criteria: Tool adoption is based on demonstrations, reviews, or peer recommendations without classroom evaluation
Does not connect coaching observations to procurement conversations
partial_indicators: Collects teacher feedback on tools and shares it informally but does not structure evaluations rigorously or connect findings to formal procurement processes

indicators.indicator_source_text: Personalize support for educators by planning and modeling the effective use of technology to improve student learning.
met_criteria: Coaching plans are tailored to each educator's context, students, and goals — not a standard programme
Models the effective use of technology in ways visible to the educator being coached
Personalises which technologies are modelled based on what serves each educator's specific students
Follows up modelling with structured reflection and planning for independent practice
not_yet_met_criteria: Coaching follows a standard pathway regardless of educator context
Does not model — only advises
Technology recommendations are generic rather than contextualised to educator and student needs
partial_indicators: Provides personalised advice but does not model practices — coaching is verbal rather than demonstrative
Models effective technology use but does not tailor the model to the specific educator's context and students

indicators.indicator_source_text: Collaborate with educators to develop authentic, active learning experiences that foster student agency, deepen content mastery and allow students to demonstrate their competency.
met_criteria: Co-designs (not just reviews) learning experiences with educators
The co-designed experience has an authentic purpose beyond the classroom
Student agency is a design criterion — students make genuine choices within the experience
Competency demonstration is embedded in the activity, not added as a separate assessment
not_yet_met_criteria: Shares lesson resources rather than co-designing with educators
The collaborative design process does not include authenticity or student agency as explicit goals
partial_indicators: Co-designs engaging and pedagogically sound experiences but authenticity is framed as 'real-world context' in the brief rather than genuine connection to an external purpose or audience

indicators.indicator_source_text: Help educators use digital tools to create effective assessments that provide timely feedback and support personalized learning.
met_criteria: Works with educators to design assessments that leverage digital tools for speed and specificity of feedback
Helps educators use assessment data from digital tools to personalise subsequent learning
Feedback cycles are designed into the assessment, not added afterward
Assessment design includes consideration of how data will be used to adjust teaching
not_yet_met_criteria: Assessment support is limited to marking and moderation — does not address feedback design or personalisation
Does not help educators leverage digital tools specifically for assessment quality or speed
partial_indicators: Helps educators use digital rubrics for clearer feedback but does not address how assessment data should be used to personalise learning or how feedback timeliness can be built into the design

indicators.indicator_source_text: Collaborate with educators to design accessible and active digital learning environments that accommodate learner variability.
met_criteria: Reviews digital learning environments against accessibility standards (not just legal minimums)
Helps educators make active design choices to accommodate diverse learners
Accessibility is a design criterion from the start, not a retrofit
The resulting environment works for the range of learners in the specific context
not_yet_met_criteria: Accessibility is treated as a compliance issue rather than a design value
Digital environments are designed for the assumed average learner — variability is not accounted for
partial_indicators: Helps educators create content with alt text and captions but does not examine the broader learning environment design for variability accommodation or ensure the environment is active rather than just accessible

indicators.indicator_source_text: Model the use of instructional design principles with educators to create effective digital learning environments.
met_criteria: Makes instructional design principles explicit when co-designing with educators
Uses terms like cognitive load, retrieval, spacing, and dual coding in context
The principles are visible in the design decisions, not just mentioned
Educators can apply the principles independently after coaching
not_yet_met_criteria: Co-designs intuitively without making the underlying instructional logic explicit
Educators walk away with a better lesson but without understanding why it works
partial_indicators: References instructional design principles in conversation but does not demonstrate them in the co-design process in ways that build educator capacity to apply them independently

indicators.indicator_source_text: Design professional learning based on needs assessments and frameworks for working with adults to support their cultural, social-emotional and learning needs.
met_criteria: Conducts a multi-method needs assessment before designing professional learning
Applies a recognised framework for adult learning (e.g., andragogy, job-embedded PD models)
Accounts for cultural and social-emotional dimensions of professional learning, not just technical content
The resulting design is demonstrably shaped by the needs assessment findings
not_yet_met_criteria: Professional learning is designed based on assumed rather than assessed needs
Does not apply adult learning frameworks — designs for teachers as if they were students
Cultural and social-emotional needs are not considered in professional learning design
partial_indicators: Sends a needs survey but designs the session based on prior plans rather than the survey data
Designs interactive sessions but does not apply explicit adult learning frameworks or account for cultural and social-emotional dimensions

indicators.indicator_source_text: Build the capacity of educators, leaders and instructional teams to put the ISTE Standards into practice by facilitating active learning and providing meaningful feedback.
met_criteria: Designs professional learning experiences where participants actively practise ISTE-aligned teaching moves
Gives specific, actionable feedback on practice during professional learning
Includes leaders and instructional teams, not just classroom teachers
Builds capacity for independent practice — the goal is transfer, not dependency on the coach
not_yet_met_criteria: Professional learning involves information transfer rather than practice and feedback
ISTE Standards are presented as content, not practised as skills
Capacity-building is not the stated or measured goal of the professional learning
partial_indicators: Facilitates active learning activities during CPD but does not provide systematic feedback on participant practice or explicitly frame the session around building capacity to put the ISTE Standards into practice

indicators.indicator_source_text: Evaluate impact of professional learning and continually make improvements in order to meet schoolwide vision for using technology for high-impact teaching and learning.
met_criteria: Has a structured impact evaluation approach that goes beyond end-of-session surveys
Measures impact at the level of practice change and student learning, not just participant satisfaction
Feeds evaluation findings back into professional learning design
Connects professional learning impact to the school's technology vision and goals
not_yet_met_criteria: Professional learning impact is evaluated through immediate satisfaction only
Evaluation is not used to improve future professional learning design
There is no connection between professional learning evaluation and institutional technology goals
partial_indicators: Collects follow-up feedback weeks after CPD and adjusts future sessions based on it, but does not measure impact at the level of classroom practice change or student learning outcomes

indicators.indicator_source_text: Model best practices for educators and leaders for securely collecting, protecting and analyzing student data.
met_criteria: Demonstrates and discusses data security practices explicitly — not just follows them
Knows what data platforms collect and how it is stored and shared
Makes data governance practices visible as a coaching topic
Helps educators understand their data responsibilities, not just their data access
not_yet_met_criteria: Data security is delegated to IT — not a coaching responsibility
Does not model or discuss data governance with educators
Focused on data analytics without addressing the governance dimension
partial_indicators: Follows data security procedures themselves but does not model or discuss these practices with educators during coaching — treats it as an IT issue rather than a shared professional responsibility

indicators.indicator_source_text: Support educators to interpret qualitative and quantitative data to inform their decisions and support individual student learning.
met_criteria: Helps educators move from 'what does the data say' to 'what should I do about it'
Supports triangulation of multiple data sources rather than reliance on a single metric
Helps educators recognise when data is misleading or when context changes its interpretation
Data interpretation leads to specific, adjusted instructional decisions
not_yet_met_criteria: Shares data dashboards with educators but does not support interpretation
Data review sessions end with observations rather than decisions
Does not help educators identify limitations or potential biases in data
partial_indicators: Supports educators in reading their data and identifying trends but does not help them evaluate data limitations, triangulate sources, or translate findings into concrete instructional adjustments

indicators.indicator_source_text: Partner with educators to empower students to use learning data to set their own goals and measure their progress.
met_criteria: Helps educators design student-facing data experiences (not just teacher-facing dashboards)
Students can access and understand their own learning data
Students use data to set specific, meaningful goals — not just acknowledge scores
The student data experience is pedagogically designed, not just a data dump
not_yet_met_criteria: Data is used to inform teacher decisions only — students have no role in interpreting or using their own data
Data conversations with students are about informing them of results, not empowering them to direct their learning
partial_indicators: Helps educators share progress data with students through reports or portals but students receive data passively — they are not guided to interpret it, set goals with it, or use it to direct their own learning strategies

indicators.indicator_source_text: Work with educators to create pathways for students to use technology to address community challenges and gain real-world experience.
met_criteria: Helps educators design community-connected technology projects with real external impact
The community connection is genuine — students interact with real stakeholders, not a simulated audience
Supports educators in managing the complexity of external partnerships
Evaluates whether student technology use in these projects builds genuine citizenship skills
not_yet_met_criteria: Community connection in learning is metaphorical or simulated, not actual
Does not help educators navigate the complexity of authentic community partnerships
partial_indicators: Helps educators design projects where students research a community issue and present findings, but the connection stops at research and presentation — students do not interact with or create something for the actual community

indicators.indicator_source_text: Collaborate with educators, leaders and students to foster inclusive online spaces and healthy balance in their use of technology.
met_criteria: Works across all three groups — educators, leaders, and students — not just one
Addresses both inclusivity and healthy balance as distinct goals
Helps audit and improve online spaces for inclusivity, not just post guidance
Supports the development of school-wide norms for healthy technology balance
not_yet_met_criteria: Digital citizenship is addressed at the student level only — educators and leaders are not included
Responds to incidents rather than proactively fostering inclusive spaces and healthy practices
partial_indicators: Works with educators to deliver digital citizenship content to students but does not engage leaders or audit platform settings to address structural factors affecting inclusivity or balance

indicators.indicator_source_text: Support educators and students to critically examine the sources and accuracy of online content and evaluate underlying assumptions, biases, and perspectives.
met_criteria: Helps educators design learning that develops genuine critical information literacy, not just surface source checking
Students are supported to identify assumptions and biases, not just inaccuracies
Critical examination is embedded in subject learning, not added as a media literacy lesson
Coaches educators to model critical evaluation themselves
not_yet_met_criteria: Source evaluation is treated as fact-checking only — deeper critical examination is not developed
Digital literacy is a compliance lesson, not a practised reasoning skill
partial_indicators: Supports educators in teaching students to identify unreliable sources using credibility checklists, but does not develop the deeper critical examination of assumptions, perspectives, and biases underpinning content

indicators.indicator_source_text: Empower educators, leaders and students to make informed decisions to protect their personal data and curate the digital profile they intend to reflect.
met_criteria: Helps all groups understand what personal data is collected by the tools they use
Supports active decision-making about digital profile curation — not just harm avoidance
Engages leaders in understanding their institutional digital footprint, not just student safety
Coaching includes practical privacy management skills, not just awareness
not_yet_met_criteria: Data privacy is treated as a youth safety topic rather than a universal professional and personal competency
Leaders and educators are not included in data literacy and digital profile work
partial_indicators: Delivers student-facing digital privacy sessions and teaches basic safety practices but does not extend this to educators and leaders, and does not develop practical profile curation skills beyond harm avoidance
